bib.title: AI Agents: The Definitive Guide, Chapter 2. Architectures and Patterns: Planning, Reactivity, and Multi-Agent-Systems

question: How do architectural patterns (structured reasoning, human-in-the-loop, supervisor, hierarchical and swarm multi-agent designs) make LLM agents plan, react and reflect reliably?
contributions: Compares single-step with multi-step ReAct execution (Table 2-1)
Shows CoT, a lightweight ToT and a ReAct loop in LangGraph code
Four human-in-the-loop interrupt patterns with LangGraph code
Supervisor, hierarchical and swarm multi-agent builds with a comparison table (Table 2-4)

results.claim: A supervisor architecture suits small teams with clear task boundaries; trade-off is a central bottleneck and single point of failure.
Swarm handoff tool create_handoff_tool passes full message history by default; filtering is optional.

limits: Early Release draft, raw and unedited; no benchmarks, only single demo runs with unreported model settings in the chapter text.
Code shown is partial; full implementations are in the book's repository and notebook, said to be activated later.
Planning at scale and tree-search algorithms are deferred to the next chapter.
Tool-trace example for Zurich weather shows a Final Answer that repeats the question in the first trace lines (printed output looks inconsistent).
practices: Give each agent a distinct role and persona to make reasoning more focused (Structured Reasoning and Action).
Use CoT prompts to externalise intermediate steps for transparency and an audit trail; it can let smaller models do harder tasks (Letting Your AI Agents Think Out Loud).
A small model proposing branches and a stronger model judging can sometimes replace a full multi-agent design, saving cost (box: ToT as an engineering shortcut).
Use ReAct when a task needs both reasoning and tool use; reasoning traces are folded back into state.
Use human-in-the-loop: approve/reject, review and edit state, review tool calls, validate human input.
Never put side-effecting code in the same node as interrupt(...); pause first, execute effects only after approval to avoid repeats on resume (box: Interrupts and side effects).
Compile with a checkpointer so interrupts can resume.
Use a supervisor for small teams, hierarchical for multi-team scale, swarm for peer handoffs (Table 2-4).
In production AgentExecutor keeps code concise; the granular graph is better for debugging.
